entries.content:
This fall a literary scandal has erupted in France around a debut novel with a dramatic title—C’était ça ou mourir (“It Was Either That or Die”)—by the Haitian-Québécois author Thélyson Orélien. Orélien’s account of a Haitian migrant’s odyssey across South and North America made it onto the best-seller list and secured nominations for all the country’s major literary awards; it was set to be translated into over twenty languages. On September 21 the novel won the Prix du Roman Fnac, an award given by France’s largest book retailer.

That same day a Twitter account called Balance ton Claude (Out your Claude) made a startling accusation. The account’s owners had run many sections of the book through the AI-detection program Pangram, they claimed, which showed widespread use of AI throughout the text. In a country where literature is still treated as a matter of national importance, the allegation got wall-to-wall media coverage and set off an acrimonious, highly politicized controversy. The prestigious Goncourt prize announced that the book had been withdrawn from consideration. Online, right-wing accounts targeted Orélien with racist invective. The Quebec newspaper La Presse reviewed some of Orélien’s older work and said it found several instances of plagiarism in columns and a short story he wrote over a decade ago. The author withdrew from public view; his publishers in Canada and France stood by him and said he was preparing evidence of his innocence.

On October 13 Orélien broke his silence with a statement in which he rejected the accusation against him as “a calumny and a heresy.” He apologized for his earlier plagiarisms, which he called “youthful mistakes,” and acknowledged that he had used AI to do research for his book. But he maintained he had used it for nothing more; he said he wrote the first draft of his novel back in 2017, and that it contained stories he had lived or heard. The book came from his guts, he wrote, and “to credit a machine for writing this text that is mine, that is of my people, is to contest not just my identity as a writer but my humanity.” On October 21 Orélien’s Canadian publisher announced that, based on the results of their own investigation, they were ending their relationship with him.

Balance ton Claude is an anonymous collective originally formed to criticize the AI-generated social media posts of politicians and business leaders. Two of the young men behind the account have come forward: Pierre-Thomas Eckert, a researcher in moral philosophy, and Samuel Fitoussi, a business manager at a venture capital company and a writer and commentator for the right-wing paper Le Figaro, where he has criticized the excesses of “wokisme.” In an editorial in Le Monde they warned of the “existential danger” that AI poses to literature, research, and human intellectual production; their goal, they claimed, was to protect the trust between writers and readers. Yet anonymously lobbing accusations online was hardly the best way to achieve such aims. In fact the Orélien debacle has exposed many currents of suspicion, mistrust, and confusion that flow through the world of French letters; more interestingly, it has opened a debate about what constitutes authorship and how literary merit is measured in the first place.

To many watching the scandal unfold, there was something suspect about the very speed and unseemly glee with which C’était ça ou mourir was denounced across right-wing accounts. “Any accusation against any one of us [writers] will be taken up immediately like a sure thing,” said the writer Virginie Despentes on a TV talk show a few days into the scandal. “As long as it comes from the far right, let’s go, it must be true!” To Orélien’s defenders, the targeting of a Black writer whose book is a sympathetic account of a migrant’s journey to safety was clearly racially and politically motivated. Why, they have asked, was this particular book analyzed? And how reliable is AI-detection software to begin with?

“Orélien does not need to justify himself,” Despentes said. “He can write as he chooses.” Many writers, she went on, “are going to use AI because AI has forced its way into our life,” integrated into word-processing applications and Internet searches. Despentes herself writes by hand in notebooks now, she added, to avoid being given constant AI-generated prompts and suggestions; her own books have been used to train LLMs. “Now I should justify myself, when AI has taken everything without my consent, without asking my opinion…. Fuck Pangram!”

In their editorial, Fitoussi and Eckert insisted that they shared their doubts about Orélien’s novel “without giving a moment’s thought to the novel’s theme, the author’s supposed opinions, and even less—it’s maddening to have to say so—to the color of his skin.” In a subsequent post on Twitter, they even wrote that people should “go easy” on Orélien and that the best thing would be for him to “get back to writing!” This show of sympathy seems highly disingenuous—they must have measured the gravity of their allegation for the writer’s career and anticipated the kind of media firestorm that would engulf him.

Advertisement

Meanwhile the debate has expanded beyond Orélien’s specific case to the future of literature in a world where editors, publishers, and readers can no longer be certain that a book is the product of a particular human consciousness. The general consensus seems to be that the literary establishment is woefully unprepared to deal with a challenge they should have seen coming. Commentators have suggested using AI-detection software as a matter of course or clearly labeling books as composed by a human or an LLM. To do the latter, the philosopher Monique Canto-Sperber wrote in Le Monde, is what honesty—and the survival of publishing—demands: “In a world in which fakes and imitations are spreading, the link between the author and his reader remains one of the rare relationships of sincerity and trust.” (EU legislation that should come into effect next year mandates that AI-generated text, audio, and video contain digital markers that will make it easier to detect.)

Others are taking a longer historical view. In an interview with the radio program France Culture, the literature professor William Marx, whose books include Adieu to Literature: History of a Devaluation (2005), noted that it has only been “since the eighteenth century that the idea of the author, tied to that of originality, has crystallized.” Nineteenth-century novelists like Alexandre Dumas still had workshops of writers assisting in their prodigious production. These early ghostwriters were called prête-plumes or, wincingly, nègres—a term that makes clear the assumed hierarchy in the ability to create, the very hierarchy that a Black writer’s commercial and critical success would upset.

Marx wondered whether we may be reaching the end of a “democratic parenthesis of literature,” an era of mass reading and writing. He envisaged a future in which the greater part of literature could be written and read by machines and only a small community would still read and write in the laborious old ways, keeping alive an art form that balances the need for expressivity and sincerity—for “the illusion of access to another soul”—and the need for formal efficacy, a full mastery of narrative and linguistic tools. Marx seems to expect, as do quite a few others, that AI will be able to master those tools fully at some point in the near future. Yet even if that did happen, readers might well continue to insist on having the first need met as well. For all the spread and popularity of AI-generated content, there remains a countervailing demand for authenticity. Part of the appeal of C’était ça ou mourir, after all, was the promise of a unique voice, grounded in the author’s own life, that could directly convey the dramatic and painful experience of migration.

Throughout the controversy, Orélien’s book has continued to sell. In late September I bought it in a bookshop in Montpellier, where it was prominently displayed with a glowing, handwritten recommendation note by the staff. Perhaps readers don’t care as much as is supposed about the use of AI; perhaps they don’t trust AI detectors any more than literary critics to tell them what is worth reading; perhaps they are simply curious.

I read the book myself with some of that same curiosity. I could not say if it was written with AI assistance; it does have many repetitions and many of those supposedly telltale sets of three. Mostly I was struck by other shortcomings.

The narrator is a Haitian history-geography professor named Jonas who on the opening pages sees his home go up in flames and his neighborhood invaded by militias. (We learn very little of the political or economic situation in Haiti—only that “the country was dead. It wasn’t a country anymore, just a pretext. A sign. A torn banknote.”) He packs a pair of underwear, a photograph of his mother, and a book of poems into a knapsack and spends the rest of the book on the move.

He also spends it describing everything he sees and experiences in highly metaphorical, lyrical terms. Here is how he presents the batey, a settlement built around a sugarcane factory:

A batey is a country within the country. A sugarcane shantytown that shelters those who have no papers and are ready to work for next to nothing—ghosts you can buy on credit. The wooden shacks line up like excuses, the tin roofs sing at the slightest rain, the dogs sleep on shoes to stay warm. Children play with bits of wood, women sell no-good doughnuts, men call each other “boss” to remember they were free once upon a time. The batey has a smell: molasses and fatigue. In it one hears the sound, day and night, of metal rubbing against resignation.

Overall, the world of the book lacks edges; it is blanketed in a soft layer of banal and sometimes nonsensical poeticization. The narrator laughs often, yet the way his laughter is described (“A dry, thin laugh, twisted like a tree that grew in a street with no sunshine”) rarely conjured any form of real laughter for me, just as I could hardly picture the neighborhood he left behind—“a giant ashtray, a cemetery without tombs, a theater of the absurd where the roles changed with every burst of gunfire.” People’s behavior is equally hard to parse. On his way out of his neighborhood Jonas sits down on the side of the road, pulls out his notebook, and writes, “Today, I lost my house, but I found my escape.” He crosses paths with a woman with two children leashed to her with a rope. She tells him: “This way, if one dies, I won’t have to look for the other.” I find it hard to imagine any mother speaking of her children this way.

Advertisement

Everyone the narrator meets gets one or two lines of this kind. When he arrives at an aunt’s house in the Dominican Republic, she asks not what happened or how long he plans to stay with her, but: “Jonas, do you think you will be able to spend your life running away?” A border guard tells him: “You have too much truth in your gaze.” On the road he tastes “the flavor of days that pass by without recognizing you”—while I couldn’t help wondering what he was actually eating, day after unemployed and wandering day. Perhaps he is meant to be a dreamy troubadour, an unreal stand-in for all those who are in search of a new home. Yet every chapter ends with the same emotional beat: poetic resignation, self-deprecating but heroic determination.

If Orélien’s editors and publishers should be taken to task, it is less for not suspecting the use of AI than for being blinded by the marketability of the author’s biography, identity, and subject matter and for trumpeting as groundbreaking a book that is quite sentimental and safe, that does little to trouble its readers’ expectations. There is nothing new in a middling book finding huge success. But the fact that so many people professed to love and be moved by a novel that may have been written with AI (to what degree and in what manner, we will likely never know) raises a troubling question: Is there anything particular, inimitable, about human intelligence and expressivity? As the French science fiction writer Alain Damasio has suggested, AI’s ability to make us doubt this is the “ultimate narcissistic wound.”

Right-wing commentators in France have had a field day compiling the exaggerated praise that the literary establishment showered on Orélien. To them it is evident that the “the left” championed him for ideological rather than literary reasons. But their own satisfaction in exposing the author and embarrassing the literary elite is also nakedly political; it has nothing to do with caring about literature. This is a sad debacle in which almost everyone has lost out, no one more than the writer himself. He is of course responsible for his own choices, but one cannot but feel sorry for Orélien. His overhyped success, glaring media exposure, and sudden fall from grace—it has all been a vertiginous process in which he has been tokenized and essentialized, made a stand-in and symbol, from all sides. He now faces the devastating brunt of an online pile-on and a national controversy.

One of the most lucid, elegant, and even-handed analyses of the debate around Orélien’s book was a Facebook post by the Senegalese writer Mohamed Mbougr Sarr, who won the Goncourt in 2021 for a marvelous novel, The Most Secret History of Men, partly inspired by an earlier literary scandal with striking parallels to the one around C’était ça ou mourir. In 1968 the Malian writer Yambo Ouologuem won a major French literary award for his novel Le devoir de violence. Accused of plagiarizing passages in the book, he said they were intended to be clear citations and had originally been in quotation marks. The scandal ended his literary career; he retired into the countryside in Mali and into silence. In his novel, Sarr imagined his own version of a Ouologuem-like figure and sent a young African writer on an obsessive search for his cursed literary forefather.

“None of what is happening is completely new,” Sarr writes in his post. “We could almost say that we are within a tradition: that of an easy doubt, or rather, a doubt that takes easily when the writer who is its object is Black.” There is nothing inherently racist about expressing concern over a Black author’s plagiarism or alleged use of AI, Sarr notes, but one cannot “minimize the racial dimensions of the accusations”—the manner in which they were made, amplified, and received.

They also seem to be part of a pattern: again and again these controversies feature authors of color. Last year in the UK Jason Arday, the youngest Black professor ever hired at Cambridge, was accused of plagiarism by another scholar who had expressed openly racist views. Cambridge opened an investigation into his work and hiring, and the British press hounded him relentlessly; Arday resigned and soon after killed himself. In the past year accusations of using LLMs have been leveled against the Caribbean writer Jamir Nazir, whose story “The Serpent in the Grove” won the Commonwealth Prize in the UK, and Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza, the Zimbabwean winner of the Caine Prize for African Writing. (Both Nazir and Kundizeza denied the allegations.) In most of these cases, the accusers have used Pangram or other AI-detection software to bolster their claims. As Sarr observes, there is a long history of such charges creating a much greater uproar when they are aimed at Black writers than at their peers, who may face similar accusations without experiencing the same consequences. “It even happens that despite confirmed plagiarism, uncredited borrowings, these authors continue to publish and to win prizes, including the most prestigious ones.”

Sarr hasn’t been the only one to point out double standards. When I discussed this article with French friends, several immediately mentioned the Algerian writer Kamel Daoud, who won the Goncourt in 2024 for his novel Houris. The protagonist of that book is a woman who has forever lost the ability to speak. When she was a child, Islamist militias fighting in the Algerian Civil War massacred her family and slit her throat, leaving her to breathe for the rest of her life through a cannula inserted in her windpipe. An Algerian woman named Saâda Arbane, who survived a similar massacre and suffers from the same condition, was a patient of Daoud’s psychiatrist wife. Arbane has sued the author in Algeria and France, claiming that he stole details of her life as well as confidential information she shared in her therapy sessions. She says that Daoud approached her about writing a book about her and that, after she declined his request, he went ahead anyway.

Daoud defended himself by casting Arbane’s allegations as a plot by the Algerian government—which he has often criticized, and which censors discussions of the civil war—to harass and silence him; the French media and literary establishment largely adopted this view and closed ranks around him in the name of supporting freedom of speech. By positioning his work first and foremost within a clash-of-civilizations discourse in France (where Daoud lives and often writes as a critical voice on Islam and Arab societies generally), he was able to almost entirely sidestep the question of whether he had committed a grave ethical violation.

There is no easy way out of deciding what a book means to us, whether it enchants us enough to make us believe in it; or of deciding who a story originally belongs to, and how much that matters. The advent of AI has exacerbated these anxieties. Sarr and others are rightly skeptical of the idea that submitting writing to AI-detection software is the way to ensure fairness or trust. To rely on such software, he wrote in his post, is to continue to nourish AI, to make it “not just a referee but a god who will decide what is human and not-human,” and to “forget that racist, condescending biases exist within the AI systems’ ways of reading and evaluating. It’s a bad idea and a huge loss of time; but above all it’s a significant loss of intellectual, political, moral autonomy,” Sarr wrote. “I read here and there that we are entering a new era of suspicion. If that is true, we are the ones creating it.”

entries.summary: Our desire to control a river’s course always conflicts with a river’s determination to shape its own.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
Late last year a team of scientists published a study in Nature comparing the biomass of wild mammals on Earth with the biomass of humans and our domesticated mammals—cattle, pigs, sheep, etc. Biomass in this sense—totaling the weight of organisms by species or habitat—is a relatively crude measure, and estimating it gets harder and harder as you go back in time and the observational record thins. The study cautiously proposes the year 1850 as a point of parity, when the biomass of humans and our domesticates roughly equaled that of wild mammals.

No one in 1850 could have sensed this conjectural state of balance, of course, and not only because the data was missing. That year came and went as most years do: humans doing their humanly thing with vanishingly little regard for other species.1 Which brings us to the present. The proportion of mammalian biomass on this planet is no longer fifty-fifty. It’s now 95 percent humans and our domesticated mammals—and only 5 percent wild mammals. How did we get here? Ever-multiplying numbers of humans2 and livestock and, in the wild, plummeting numbers in every class of species, including mammals.

If this were science fiction, we might imagine Earth’s human inhabitants coming together, long before it was far too late, to consider ways of protecting and sharing the planet’s riches with all the other organisms. The truly fictional element in a tale like that would be humans actually committing to global, equitable interspecies sharing—and then sticking to it from generation to generation. But such things simply aren’t in the “nature” of Capitalist Earth Homo sapiens, whose nature it is to believe that only our nature matters.

How large a share of Earth’s natural resources are humans entitled to? That’s an ecological question. But it’s also a philosophical and ethical one, and it was thoughtfully articulated by the fourth American president, James Madison. (This was once upon a time, when a president could be articulate, philosophical, and ethical all at once.) In May 1818, a year after he left office, Madison gave a talk to the Albemarle, Virginia, Agricultural Society titled “The Role of Agriculture in Civilization.” In it he explains what must have seemed evident to his audience once it was stated: civilization and agriculture are inextricably and beneficially linked. And then he adds these remarkable words. Their formality may sound unfamiliar, but they contain a powerful and prescient thought:

We can scarcely be warranted in supposing that all productive powers of [Earth’s] surface can be made subservient to the use of man, in exclusion of all the plants and animals not entering into his stock of sustenance; that all the elements & combinations of elements, in the earth, the atmosphere, and the water, which now support such various & such numerous descriptions of created beings animate and inanimate, could be…appropriated to the exclusive [support] and increase of the human part of the creation; so that the whole habitable earth [should] be as full of people as the spots most crowded now are, or might be made; & as destitute as those spots are of the plants & animals not used by man.

In other words, humans are not warranted to do the very thing we’re doing: stripping the planet for the apparent benefit of our species alone. Madison seems to speak with an implicit understanding that all other organisms have a right to their vital share of the world habitat.3 It’s almost as though he were reading the pattern of history and the explosive growth of his new nation through the eyes of other creatures.

Madison has something else on his mind as well: the surprisingly porous border—in one direction only—between “civilization” and the lifeways of Native Americans. He points out a persistent irony in the America of 1818: how easily “civilized” people, i.e., white and of European descent, succumbed to “the charms of that personal independence which belongs to the uncivilized State”—how willingly, in other words, they abandoned “civilization” for what Madison calls “the indolence enjoyed by those who subsist on the mere bounties of nature.”4 He argues, in fact, that there’s “a disinclination in human nature, to exchange the savage for the Civilized State.”

These very themes are central to the work of James C. Scott, the brilliant Yale anthropologist and political scientist who died, age eighty-seven, in July 2024, a few months before the publication of his final book, In Praise of Floods: The Untamed River and the Life It Brings. Scott, too, is interested in the “Civilized State.”5 In Madison’s phrase, “state” means the condition of being civilized. But to Scott it means the state: the structures of power and governance that bind a governed people—and the source of “both our freedoms and our unfreedoms.”

Advertisement

As for agriculture, it gave rise, in Scott’s view, not to civilization broadly, as Madison uses the word, but to early versions of the state, which strove (as it still strives, in different ways)

to create a legible, measured, and fairly uniform landscape of taxable grain crops and to hold on this land a large population available for corvée labor, conscription, and, of course, grain production.

In contrast, the yields from “pastoralism or shifting agriculture” were much harder to count or commandeer, as were the “mobile peoples” who engaged in them and who preferred a peripheral relationship with the state. “Putting it epigraphically,” Scott writes, “there is sedentary grain growing without the state but there is no early state without sedentary farming.” Scott encourages the reader to wonder, as he does, just how we humans came to be “cereal-growing, livestock-rearing subjects governed by the novel institution we now call the state”—an institution that in Scott’s accurate view is “determined to refashion nature for the benefit of a single species.”

Like Madison, Scott discerns a counternarrative to the historical story so often told: the familiar march of progress “upwards” from “primitive” hunter-gatherers living in small kinship groups to inhabitants (free and unfree) of an early grain-fed state to, well, us. The rise of the first Mesopotamian city-states circa 3500 BCE

6 surely didn’t look like “progress.” Compared with the lifeways of hunter-gatherers, Scott writes, the shift to sedentary agriculture led to “a contraction of our species’ attention to and practical knowledge of the natural world, a contraction of diet, a contraction of space, and perhaps a contraction, as well, in the breadth of ritual life.”

An autonomous, non-state existence—Madison would have called it uncivilized or “savage”—had much more to offer than personal independence and an escape from the drudgery and “unremitting toil of plough agriculture and livestock rearing.” It provided a more diverse diet as well as freedom from the diseases, zoonotic and otherwise, that emerged when humans and their domestic animals began crowding together in fixed settlements. It was as if, to use Scott’s image, humans had abandoned a rich biological and nutritional “library” for an impoverished one—as if, in fact, humans had been domesticated by the plants and animals they had domesticated.

The early rise of agriculture, Scott argues, did more “to depress standards of human welfare than to raise them.” Going over to the barbarians7—living outside the state and adapting to what Scott calls “agro-ecology”—was “far more common than any of the standard civilizational narratives allow for.” That’s one of the problems with “hegemonic human-centered narratives.” They intentionally ignore counternarratives that don’t culminate in the status quo, while also ignoring “the fate of the myriad of nonhuman life forms.”

A river runs through Scott’s “long essay on rivers,” In Praise of Floods. It is the Ayeyarwady,8 which flows some 1,350 miles through Scott’s beloved Burma9 (where he spent two years after college and returned often between 2010 and 2020) before debouching into the Andaman Sea through distributaries in its delta. The Ayeyarwady is not the untamed river of Scott’s subtitle, for the human impact on the river, like so many others around the globe, has been immense and deeply unfortunate. Its floodplains have been deforested, causing unchecked erosion. Its water is being contaminated by runoff from fertilizer and pesticides, poisoned by the chemicals used in gold mining, and disrupted by turbulence and warming caused by other forms of unregulated mining. The riverbed is being commercially dredged for sand and gravel, with appalling consequences for riverine habitats. Its waters are pumped and siphoned for irrigation, and its floodplains have been drained, contributing to what some environmental scientists call “the Great Drying,” a widespread phenomenon that seems to occur wherever humans have encountered wetlands. Dikes and embankments and irrigation dams have “penned in the river,” Scott writes, and the military junta is even now reviving plans to build a massive hydroelectric dam, sponsored by China, at the confluence that forms the Ayeyarwady10—a project blocked in 2011 by public outcry.

And yet the Ayeyarwady lives, allowing Scott to summon “a parliament” of unexpected voices in a chapter called “Nonhuman Species.” Rising, metaphorically, one by one to speak to the reader are members of several of the species most at risk in the river. They include the Ayeyarwady river dolphin (the interlocutor), two kinds of fish—the snow carp and the hilsa—the Burmese roofed turtle, the oriental darter, the Asian hairy-nosed otter, the mollusk, and even the white ginger plant. Scott doesn’t devise an individual idiom for each of these “riverine citizens”—they all speak with his precision. But the effect is powerful. It creates what I think of as interspecies parallax—a sudden shift in perspective from the perceptual (and ethical) world of one species to the perceptual (and ethical) world of another.

Advertisement

One after another, these nonhuman speakers give first-person voice to fears and complaints that closely echo those of the Burmese people who work and live along the Ayeyarwady: loss of habitat, rapidly worsening pollution, overexploitation, the inanition of the stream itself. At the root of everything they say lies the threat of extinction: loss of habitat, loss of a way of life, loss of life itself. Their complaint against our species is fundamental and well founded. Says the dolphin about humans, “You declared the territory aqua nullius and terra nullius—water and land belonging to no one and therefore open to your claim of exclusive sovereignty over all forms of life.”

In a way, the nonhuman voices speaking from the Ayeyarwady resemble the animal voices that speak in the remarkable tenth-century Arabic text called The Case of the Animals Versus Man Before the King of the Jinn. The animals in that fable bring humankind to trial for our endless depredations of the natural world. As they speak they indict Homo sapiens and at the same time present an encyclopedic natural history examining the character and diversity of the animal creation. What’s surprising in both Scott’s book and The Case of the Animals is the reasonableness, the inherent wisdom, the patience and understanding of the speakers—from all classes of animals—as they discuss the problem of our abusive species. They sound perhaps the way animals wish humans sounded but rarely do. As the trial in The Case of the Animals nears its end, for instance, a human orator “from Mecca and Medina” sums up the defense of Homo sapiens by saying flatly, as if it were beyond question, “These animals are slaves to us and we are their masters and owners.” To which the nightingale says, simply, no: “You stand on equal footing with us.”

On the Ayeyarwady, there’s also another class of beings to consider, the nats: spirits that belong to and inhabit the riverscape. The nats were once humans who over time became “revered spirits,” each with its own highly localized, often tragic, sometimes heroic story. Both “benign and malicious,” the nats “exert enormous power over the fate of all riverine creatures.” These aren’t quaint spiritual emanations, rising like mist from the Ayeyarwady. They say little or nothing, but they act, and act in ways that demand from river dwellers attention and propitiation. As Scott says, they’re “worshiped, placated, evaded, and invoked.” They’ve also played an important part in local traditions that “were vital in maintaining the ecological balance of the river and ensuring a healthy fish population,” traditions that under the pressure of “economic hardships and political instability” are themselves becoming extinct, with dismaying effect.

When its turn comes to speak in In Praise of Floods, the white ginger plant (Curcuma candida) makes an important point. “We are creatures of the in-between,” it says, referring to its species’ love of swamps and marshes. Scott, who calls himself “a student of resistance,” is also, necessarily, a student of the connection between resistance and the geography and ecology of the in-between. In the binary view of the mapmaker or state official, what isn’t dry land must be water, and vice versa. But what fascinates Scott are the places that are sometimes land, sometimes water, and often mud: floodplains, alluvial islands in the Ayeyarwady, the Ayeyarwady Delta, and wetlands of every kind. These are places of extraordinary biological diversity, which declines rapidly as you move away from them. They’re also places of biological and geomorphic resistance, defying the human desire to create a vastly simplified “state-serving habitat.” In times past they were refugia for people who chose for their own reasons to become or remain illegible to the state, creating “potential sites of resistance and rebellion.” All of these in-betweens are replenished, along untamed rivers, by the bounty of periodic flooding.

Reading In Praise of Floods, I recalled a passage from Mark Twain’s Life on the Mississippi. In his opening pages, Twain describes the river’s habit of making “prodigious jumps” and finding new channels. The Mississippi, he writes, “is always changing its habitat bodily—is always moving bodily sidewise.” We don’t tend to talk of planetary features like rivers as having habitats. We say that they are habitats or provide or create them. They are, you might say, the ground of habitat itself. But thinking of a river as having a habitat helps us reimagine its natural dynamism and its complex relation to the terrain it rises from and through which it flows. It helps us see a river as a living being11 which, in its natural state, explores its habitat and alters it, as all organisms do. This is Scott’s task in his final opus: describing the natural habitat of rivers and “the assemblage of life-forms that depend on the river for their existence and well-being.” As it happens, only one of those life-forms is us.

We think of rivers as having a unitary, linear course, however sinuous they may be, as if a river could be nothing more than its main channel. But a river is not merely its main channel, and certainly not its main channel as delineated on a map. In a radical sense, a river can’t be mapped definitively because a map projects the present into the future. As Scott, echoing Twain, notes, there’s no assuming “that the present course of a river is an adequate description of its future.” Nor is a river merely water flowing downhill along its bed from a single source—a vision of fluvial geography that sparked the mid-nineteenth-century search for the origin of the Nile. A river doesn’t simply flow from a single source through a landscape on its way to somewhere else. It shapes the landscape and gathers it. Its sources are innumerable. It draws moisture of every kind—from “wetlands, damp soils, tiny puddles, ice, dew, and groundwater”—to itself, connecting them as “elements of a single hydrological system.” “Properly viewed,” writes Scott, “it is the entire waterscape that comprises what we conventionally call a river.”

The most important element in that waterscape is periodic inundation—flooding—which redistributes the waters a river has gathered and benefits every organism it touches. As the white ginger says, its species needs “the rich, nutritious mud brought to us annually by the flood pulse.”12 The ginger might well be speaking on behalf of every organism in the floodplain, including the very earliest farmers, who practiced “flood-retreat” agriculture. As the water receded, they found in the floodplain the richest possible soil—“nutritious mud”—renewed by the river year after year without any effort on their part until at last the floodplain was taken over for other purposes and lost its character.

To every form of control, a river offers resistance, unless it’s been functionally extinguished, like the lower stretches of the Rio Grande and the Colorado, which no longer flow all the way to their deltas. To borrow a word from Dilip da Cunha’s The Invention of Rivers (2018), a river dissents. No matter how energetically humans pursue their war to prevent flooding and “exterminate mud” (Scott’s italics), the kinetic energy we borrow to generate hydropower—at immense cost to riverine ecology—is always pushing at the boundaries humans erect to keep a river in what we believe should be its place. As the always illuminating Ellen Wohl writes in Following the Bend: How to Read a River and Understand Its Nature (2025), we’ve “been remarkably persistent, thorough, and in some respects, successful at transforming rivers into something unnatural and unsustainable.” But confined is just what a river will not be, not for long.

Trying to prevent all flooding by means of “flow regulation”—the ancient, endless, universal, and unceasing building of dikes and levees and dams—has always come “at the cost of laying the groundwork for more catastrophic floods” (Scott’s italics). Flood prevention creates the kind of feedback loop plainly visible in the historic American effort to prevent all wildfires—a practice that merely amasses the fuel for more damaging future burns. There’s an important point here. If humans were to try to prevent earthquakes, it’s hard to imagine we might make them worse than they are. Same for typhoons or tornadoes or tsunamis. But nearly everything we’ve done—and are still doing—to prevent flooding makes flooding worse, makes the flood pulse more violent. Floods are now almost entirely anthropogenic. This isn’t only a function of anthropogenic climate change and its worrying effects on the hydrological cycle.13 Our desire to control a river’s course always conflicts with a river’s determination to shape its own.

Movement, variation, instability, disturbance, resistance—these are the very qualities Scott emphasizes in the behavior of rivers and in riverine ecology, in contrast to the official state desire to convert rivers into pipelines or aqueducts incapable of flooding. His goal in In Praise of Floods is “to disturb any static understanding of the river.” Scott’s approach differs radically from the way we conventionally understand rivers. It’s as though millennia ago our species adopted a riverine policy best expressed in words attributed to Joseph Stalin: “Water which is allowed to enter the sea is wasted.” To this we seem to have added a corollary: water that’s allowed to enter the sea unpolluted is doubly wasted. If Stalin’s words seem too harsh, consider instead a statement by Herbert Hoover in 1926, when he was secretary of commerce. The purpose of federal oversight of American rivers, he wrote, was the “coordinated long-view development of each river system to its maximum utilization.” This is the bureaucratic version of Stalin’s anti-ecological dogmatism. Putting it epigraphically (as Scott might say), it’s hard to beat these words from the US Bureau of Reclamation in the 1930s: “Total control for greater Wealth.”

“What we have done to rivers,” Scott writes, “seems a powerful metaphor for understanding the troubled and possibly cataclysmic relationship between humans and nature generally.” He quotes Theodor Schwenk, a water researcher and the author of Sensitive Chaos: The Creation of Flowing Forms in Water and Air (1962). Schwenk registers the fact that humans can no longer look “at the being of water but merely at its physical value.” And he has this to say about our planetary predicament: “A way of thinking that is directed solely to what is profitable cannot perceive the vital coherence of all things in nature.” The fact that in rivers this vital coherence emerges in the midst of movement, variation, instability, and disturbance makes our efforts to impose “stasis, regularity, and predictability” upon them—upon all the world’s natural systems—look even more pathetic and tragic. As Scott writes, the landscapes we now live in “are engineered for a single purpose: to satisfy the taste and needs of a single species.”

Very few of us have ever seen a wild or “untamed” river, undammed, unsiphoned, unleveed, free flowing. They still do flow—a few of them—in relatively inaccessible places like the far north and parts of Central Africa and South America. And though the United States was once rich in in-between places (“approximately 221 million acres of wetlands—an area more than twice the size of California—at the time of European settlement”), very few of us have ever seen what might be called a living floodplain. So why go on talking about these things? Why make such an effort to understand a world none of us has ever lived in? Why try to remember what isn’t part of our personal memory?

Let me suggest two reasons. Trying to understand the richness, the biotic wealth of a former world makes it plain that our species, especially in the last few centuries, has been conducting a brutal, undeclared war on diversity. We can pretend that the social and cultural diversity humans have created—itself now under threat—can somehow substitute for biological diversity. Nothing could be further from the truth. The second reason is this: I believe we owe a nearly infinite debt to nature—a debt to the natural world in which we evolved. This is a debt we can only try to repay by our actions. Yet we’ve acted—and still act—as though the natural world has somehow contracted an irredeemable debt to us, giving us the right and duty to extract repayment in every way we can.

Reading In Praise of Floods, you’ll inevitably find yourself thinking about resistance. It may occur to you that there came a point, ages ago, when we began to treat humans—peoples—the same way we treat biotic communities in the natural world. As Scott makes plain, resistance is fundamental to life, fundamental to holding open a space for living. You may never have expected to feel the need to resist. But here we are.

entries.title: Multiplying Selves
entries.summary: In How It Works Out, a couple reappears in alternate realities—as celebrities, parents, cannibals, pets and insects—in search of the best of possible worlds.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
“For any event, there is an infinite number of possible outcomes. Our choices determine which outcomes will follow. But there is a theory in quantum physics that all possibilities that can happen or could happen do happen in alternate quantum realities.” This summary of the many-worlds interpretation of quantum physics, a theory first proposed by the American physicist Hugh Everett in the 1950s, is given by a sentient android named Data serving as an officer on the Federation starship USS Enterprise. Technically it’s delivered by the actor Brent Spiner, performing as Data, at a pivotal moment in “Parallels,” an episode from the seventh and final season of Star Trek: The Next Generation. In that episode Data’s fellow officer Worf, a Klingon, returns to the Enterprise after some time spent at an intergalactic sports competition, only to discover that he has passed through a hole in space-time—there’s always a hole in space-time—and that the reality he now inhabits is different from the one he left, in ways that are subtle and profound, comic and tragic.

Most strictly scientific formulations of the many-worlds interpretation hold that there is no practical way to move between branching quantum realities, or even to prove that these alternate realities exist, except as far-out mathematical possibilities. For Star Trek, getting Worf back to his home reality is as simple as flying back through that pesky space-time fissure, then sealing it with a blast from the ship’s engines.

While the theory has been the subject of intense debate within the scientific community—Stephen Hawking and Richard Feynman believed it to be likely true; the Nobel Prize–winning Dutch physicist Gerard ’t Hooft has rejected it as implausible—popular culture has run away with the idea of a multiverse in which every possible iteration of reality can coexist. In recent years, superhero movie franchises have become jittery, reality-hopping narratives of rebooting, recycling, and reincarnation, grafting the idea of infinitely branching realities onto old-fashioned tales of good guys punching bad guys. Setting your stories within a multiverse creates the opportunity for endless marketable derivatives: if a beloved character is killed in one film, you simply open up an inter-universal portal and let them stroll back in during the next.

On a less mercenary, more personal level, exploring alternate realities is a deeply human urge. Most of us, especially in moments of stress or depression, picture other careers, other partners, other selves, often looking for the decisions that allowed our current circumstances to come into being. We don’t always do this in a posture of regret: sometimes we want to confirm the thesis that the life we are currently living is, in fact, the best of all possible lives. Or, at least, not one of the worst.

How It Works Out, a raunchy, hilarious, and occasionally unsettling debut novel in stories by the Canadian writer Myriam Lacroix, is filled with exactly these kinds of speculation. The book is a literary cabinet of curiosities, from which spill alternate realities in ways that are as thunderingly literal and self-consciously silly as any episode of Star Trek but that are also clever, surprising, and deeply felt.

Lacroix grew up in Montreal and now lives in Vancouver with her partner, Allison. That kind of personal detail may seem irrelevant in a book review, but it’s important for understanding Lacroix’s debut, in which the stories are linked by the names of their main characters: Myriam and Allison, who are presented as different people in each tale but who often share biographical facts with the writer and her real-life partner. (How much any of these fictional Myriams and Allisons resemble the actual ones we can only guess and, in the case of the book’s darker stories, hope that the answer is “not much.”)

To describe what happens in How It Works Out is to risk getting lost in an appellative tangle. For example, there is the real-life Myriam Lacroix, the one who is the author of the book, and then there is the Myriam Lacroix of “The Sequel,” the book’s fifth story. That Myriam is a mentally troubled former barista who achieved enormous cultural, critical, and financial success with a book called How It Works Out: Building a Healthy Lesbian Relationship in the Patriarchy, which she cowrote with her partner, Allison. This fictional version of How It Works Out is uncompromisingly political. “Even lesbians who succeed at marriage ultimately fail,” the book asserts, “for they have succeeded only in infiltrating an institution that hates them.”

The book was a best seller, we learn, with copies “on every queer woman’s shelf.” But now, a decade after its publication, sales have evaporated. The culture has shifted; those queer women’s bookshelves have been cleared to make room for even more uncompromising manifestos. “The new generation doesn’t find us radical enough,” Allison, the story’s narrator, tells us. “Nobody cares if a couple of Canadian lesbians have a happy ending.” Their agent, Steve, however, has a plan that involves the kind of rebranding attempted by many C-list celebrities in the era of Trump. Allison sums it up:

Advertisement

If we can’t win over the queer feminists, we might have a chance with the right-wing lesbians, the gated-community dykes. They’re the ones with disposable income, anyway. First step was to get married, get the media’s attention, show publishers the names Myriam and Allison still mean something.

At the moment when Allison says “I do” in a lavish ceremony at a luxe hotel in the mountains, she has trouble staying focused, given all that is happening to make the event go viral: “I’m distracted by the Elle Canada photographer, whose finger is going at the shutter button like she’s trying to get it off. Steve is typing like crazy on his phone, live-tweeting.” Allison is the more fame-skeptical and emotionally grounded of the pair, but she’s not above a bit of clickbaiting of her own: when she kisses her new bride, she slips in “some tongue for the press,” then takes care to smile in a way that shows off her “crooked canine, which some internet forums agree is my best attribute.”

Steve’s rebranding strategy appears, at first, to go well: the actor Kristen Stewart retweets one of the wedding photos; #MAwedding and #howitworksout start trending. But then Myriam, who suffers from extreme fits of paranoia and fear, becomes ill after eating a salad, and Allison begins an intense affair with the doctor who treats her. The story then jumps ahead in time, positing a future in which Myriam is out of the picture and Allison has achieved fame with her second wife, the doctor, with whom she has had a baby. The story ends with the happy couple dancing on set with Ellen DeGeneres before a live studio audience, as confetti falls from the ceiling.

The satire in “The Sequel” is as dark as it is meta. (And it is very meta: the real-life Canadian lesbian sister pop duo Tegan and Sara, who blurbed the actual Lacroix’s actual book, make a cameo in the story as the kind of bored, cynical celebrities who get paid to hang out at weddings.) The gags are so sharp, it’s possible to miss the more thoughtful story happening behind them. Lacroix (the real-life one) wants to do more than merely skewer the most obvious excesses of 2024-era clout chasing. The Allison character, though she is a willing partner in the rebranding, mostly goes along with it because she is fighting to stay close to Myriam, whose illnesses and obsessions threaten to dissolve all the joy left in their relationship. Remove the cultural fame, the agent, and the celebrity wedding, and she is any partner attempting Hail Mary passes to find their way back to what they had before, to fly the spaceship back through the hole in space-time.

Given that Lacroix is a relative unknown in the literary world, the sheer audacity of building her first book from funhouse-mirror distortions of her own life is impressive. Imagine Nicolas Cage playing up his own outsize persona in a film like The Unbearable Weight of Massive Talent (2022) before having starred in anything else. How It Works Out could have easily turned out a pointless, self-indulgent mess. But Lacroix presents her outrageous scenarios as settled facts, without any special pleading or giving the reader an opportunity for doubt. The opening of the book’s first story, “The Meaning of Life,” contains all these strengths in compressed form:

They’d planned on getting beer from Toby’s, but instead they got a baby, and they were not unhappy about it. Myriam and Allison hadn’t talked about kids yet, but finding one seemed to be a sign that it was time. Besides, being lesbians, this spared them the trouble of adopting or getting one of their friends to have sex with them.

Here, as she does throughout the book, Lacroix writes with a mixture of emotional coolness and disarming jokiness. The tossed-off gags seem to signal, “Hey, everything’s OK here, reader,” when it quickly becomes apparent that everything is not: the comic shrug in that last line allows us to accept the freakish behavior that follows without the sense of judgment that might be prompted by a more dour literary reality.

In this version of the Myriam–Allison relationship, the pair are the kind of hip, young urbanites who spot an old couch and immediately wonder “if they could turn it into some sort of art installation.” They are also the kind of people who, having found a baby in an alleyway, decide to take it home and name it Jonah, because “they had no idea what Jonahs were like, and they liked the element of surprise.” Taking care of a baby challenges and deepens their understanding of the world. “Nuclear families were a concept made up by the same people who wanted you to get full-time jobs or sell your art for money,” Myriam thinks. “Still, when she lifted Jonah from Allison’s heaving chest and held him in her arms, she could feel the exact dimensions of her happiness, its weight and humid breath. It wasn’t a dream.”

Advertisement

It turns out that Baby Jonah belongs to Dina, an unhappy woman who lost track of her kid while her husband, Ken, was getting beaten up for obnoxiously heckling a comedian. The loss of her child causes the already miserable Dina to crash emotionally, but also brings her newfound clarity: “Realizing that she felt like shit was a bit better than feeling like shit but being too dissociated to realize it. Now, if she started to punch her steering wheel, she knew why she was punching it.”

The Myriam–Allison and Dina–Ken pairings in the story are stereotypes, if not quite caricatures. (Ken, true to clichéd form, is a foulmouthed and lazy brute who sits on his basement-apartment couch spouting homophobic curses while watching hockey; the presence of a stained undershirt is not explicitly mentioned, but it can be inferred.) This flattening of character is intentional: the story, despite its moments of violence, plays out like a fable, with Dina deciding to leave Ken and join the girls in raising Jonah. These people inhabit a gauzy fantasy world, which belies the fact that the story is about a young couple kidnapping an abandoned baby.

The soft focus of that first story works as a setup for the nightmare of the next, “Love Bun,” in which Myriam is a depressed postgraduate being supported by Allison as she struggles to complete a “thesis on trauma, and the cycle of abuse, in the works of certain realist writers.” After a cooking accident, Myriam discovers that eating a small slice of Allison’s flesh makes her feel “giddy and light, like I’d been pumped full of helium.” It also sharpens other appetites: “Three orgasms later, I ate an entire bowl of penne primavera.”

Shortly after that incident, Allison loses a finger in an ice-skating mishap, and Myriam does the unthinkable: she keeps the finger and eats it raw. (It has a “tangy umami flavor.”) The effect is immediate:

It felt like emerging from some sort of primordial glue. I could smell the flowers under the snow, waiting to be born. An elderly woman smiled and I could see behind her teeth, into her throat, down her esophagus, right inside the pouch of her stomach, where love was brewing like a dark green potion. Love was everywhere. Rows of shops sprung out of the sidewalk like pages from a pop-up book, bricks so bright with their own light I could hardly look.

It gets worse. Myriam and Allison decide to have children, whom, with a grim sense of inevitability, they eat—only taking tiny nibbles of some of them, consuming others whole. The cannibalistic descriptions in the story are vivid, difficult to read, and visceral (literally so). It is here that Lacroix’s approach most resembles the horror-infused literary parables often associated with writers like Carmen Maria Machado (Her Body and Other Parties), Kristen Roupenian (Cat Person and Other Stories), and Rachel Yoder (Nightbitch). Lacroix does not spare the violence or the blood, but even as the horrors of “Love Bun” are compounding, she keeps the jokes coming: the depraved couple name their children things like Framboise and Kale. When their firstborn, Jonah—Lacroix’s book is lousy with callbacks—gets a life sentence for eating a male friend, Allison blames the verdict on homophobia. (These stories, incidentally, serve as an excellent corrective to the claims that “wokeism” has taken all the edge out of comedy: How It Works Out is uncompromising and exact in its targeting of people on all sides of various culture wars, and yet manages never to punch down.)

“Love Bun” represents the most extreme and horrifying variation on Myriam–Allison. (The oddest is “Mantis,” in which Allison is a pet dog, Myriam a pet mantis in a terrarium.) The levels of surrealism change from story to story, though in almost all of them reality feels both heightened and warped. The interpersonal dynamics shift, too: sometimes Myriam is the villain, sometimes it’s Allison, sometimes both. The one constant is that at least one of the partners yearns for the other. Even in its strangest scenarios, the Myriams and Allisons of How It Works Out exhibit the most basic of needs, the need for love.

The answers to whether any of these variants actually fulfill this need range from “of course” to “of course not,” but even in the book’s darkest moments, there is no doubt that love is worth struggling for. This romantic core, though often buried under much cultural and personal rubble, is what distinguishes Lacroix’s book from the more pessimistic visions of Roupenian et al. These are dark stories, but they have an undeniably sentimental heart, which keeps them from feeling like too clever experiments. Even when the Myriams and Allisons are presented as monsters, we somehow want them to be together, and feel genuine sadness when they can’t manage it. As for the fate of the actual Myriam and Allison, that is somewhat spoiled by the book’s dedication page: “To Allison, I figured it out. I know how it works out.”
