entries.title: Picture This
entries.summary: Throughout the history of print, illustrators have helped visualize writer’s stories, and at times became storytellers themselves.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
Henry James loved pictures, but not when they threatened to supplement his words. For James, “responsible prose” should be “pictorial enough, above all in itself”—the phrase comes from his preface to The Golden Bowl (1909)—and anything that offered to relieve it of that responsibility risked short-circuiting the process by which good writers should stimulate the imaginative capacity of their readers. “As regards illustrations you will of course please yourself,” he observed resignedly to the editor of The Century Magazine, Robert Underwood Johnson, in 1887. “I frankly confess that I hate them when attached to my own prose—& like them only as an incident of that of others.”

James lost that particular battle when The Century published the travel essay in question, “London,” with thirteen illustrations by the American artist Joseph Pennell the following year. But with the partial exception of the frontispieces that Scribner’s commissioned from the photographer Alvin Langdon Coburn for the so-called New York Edition of 1907–1909, James mostly succeeded in keeping his novels and tales free of illustration. Writing about visual art was one thing—the narrator of a story also submitted to The Century in 1887 happens to be a portrait painter—but James preferred that the magazine print “The Liar” “pictureless,” as he put it with characteristic emphasis to Johnson. “Ah, your illustrations—your illustrations,” he exclaimed wryly, “how, as a writer, one hates ’em; & how their being as good as they are makes one hate ’em more!”

James’s resistance to illustration doesn’t figure in D.B. Dowd’s new history of the practice, Reading Pictures, though the writer who liked such images well enough when they accompanied the work of others does make two brief appearances, both quotations from his 1893 collection of essays on the subject, Picture and Text. Though the evidence Dowd has assembled suggests that James was clearly exaggerating when he announced at the outset that “the illustration of books, and even more of magazines, may be said to have been born in our time,” the novelist wasn’t wrong to think that he lived in a century when words and images could be combined in increasingly profitable ways and that publishers were eager to take advantage of the opportunity.

According to the Oxford English Dictionary, it was also in the nineteenth century that the word “illustration”—which originally meant “spiritual enlightenment” or “illumination”—took on the modern sense of a pictorial representation. One of the dictionary’s earliest examples of this new usage, dated 1817, would have resonated with James, since it refers to the engravings after Richard Westall that served as frontispieces for the collected works of Sir Walter Scott, a publishing milestone that in turn provided a principal model for James’s New York Edition and its very different frontispieces almost a hundred years later. It was in James’s time, too, that the professional illustrator was first named as such, at least in English, which Dowd dates to the middle of the century.

Dowd’s book ranges chronologically from the ninth century to the present and geographically from East Asia to America; its more than four hundred images include everything from Buddhist scrolls and illuminated manuscripts to advertising calendars, album covers, and comic strips. Despite its subtitle, this history of illustration isn’t so much a sequential narrative as a series of loosely arranged mini-histories and thematic excurses, some more sharply focused than others. But central to Reading Pictures, both literally and figuratively, is what Dowd calls “the high season of illustrated mass publishing,” which began in the late nineteenth century and continued well into the twentieth. “Illustrations,” he begins by stipulating, are “printed, by definition,” and though a few of the images in his study appear to violate that rule—an oil painting of a fight scene by George Bellows from 1909, for instance, or a drawing by Molly Crabapple of construction workers in Gaza that was apparently published online in 2015—the vast majority of the illustrations in Reading Pictures were first disseminated in print.

What that meant, however, differed markedly over time and from one culture to another. Dowd’s earliest example is dated 868 CE and comes from a seventeen-foot-long Buddhist scroll whose elegant ideographs, like its images, were printed from fixed wooden blocks rather than the movable type that European broadsides and books typically began to combine with woodcuts in the aftermath of Gutenberg’s invention nearly six centuries later. (Such single-block printing is known as xylography, from the Greek xylon, meaning wood or timber.) Though the Gutenberg Bible was not illustrated, a German publisher quickly took advantage of the new technology to issue a book entitled Der Edelstein (The Gemstone, 1461), in which illustrated fables from classical sources were retold in the vernacular by a Dominican monk named Ulrich Boner. As if to advertise the possibilities of the new medium, the monk’s woodcut figure appeared at the beginning of each fable, helpfully pointing to the accompanying image.

Advertisement

Around the same time, European printmakers also began to exploit the potential of copper engraving, a practice that seems to have originated with an anonymous artist known as the Master of the Playing Cards before largely migrating to the reproduction of paintings and sculptures in the seventeenth century. Though the use of chemicals rather than a burin to cut through the plate made the process of etching comparatively faster and more fluid, both of these so-called intaglio methods were more laborious than woodcutting, and both produced prints that had to be tipped or bound into letterpress books, since neither could be simultaneously employed with movable type. Eighteenth-century publishers might supplement their editions of poets and dramatists with engraved illustrations, but such volumes typically remained luxury items. The development of white-line engraving, a technique first perfected by the British artist Thomas Bewick, eventually helped to bring down costs by allowing engravers to incise refined marks directly into durable wooden blocks that could then be used for relief printing.

Bewick is probably most familiar to modern readers as the artist whose depictions of birds and their far-flung origins so fascinate the young heroine in the opening paragraphs of Charlotte Brontë’s Jane Eyre (1847). But his technique really came into its own a few years before the novel was published, when an enterprising editor named Herbert Ingram launched The Illustrated London News (1842), a weekly broadside whose combination of pictures and text—thirty-two wood engravings in each sixteen-page issue—proved especially popular for war reporting. Within a year of its founding, there were French and German equivalents, both also with versions of the word “illustrated” in their titles, and they were followed in the next decade by Frank Leslie’s Illustrated Newspaper (1855) and Harper’s Weekly (1857), among others, in the US.

Like the Crimean War, the American Civil War afforded ample opportunities for the men known as “special artists” to ply their trade, transmitting images directly from the battlefield to their subscribers—or more precisely to the engravers who helped translate their drawings and watercolors into print. (Illustration, as Dowd emphasizes, is a “team sport.”) Though we might imagine that such work was soon overtaken by the camera, that does not appear to have been the case: readers seem to have grown accustomed to the clarity and interpretive power of engraved images, and “for decades after it was possible to print halftone photographs in newspapers,” Dowd reports, “editors declined to do so.”

Indeed, one of the reasons Dowd’s history can sometimes be hard to follow is the unevenness of the phenomena he analyzes. While the visual culture on which he focuses clearly depended on technological changes, these didn’t necessarily succeed one another in chronological order, nor did they migrate consistently from place to place. Even in the West, xylographic books didn’t die out with Gutenberg, as the multiplying word bubbles in two scenes from Life and Acts of St. John the Evangelist (circa 1465–1470) richly demonstrate, while Japanese publishers soon abandoned the movable type imported by the Jesuits in the late sixteenth century and reverted to the use of single blocks that printed calligraphic marks and images simultaneously. In China, too, single-block printing didn’t give way until the introduction of modern lithography in the 1870s, and despite the widespread use of wood engraving in Europe and North America, the Chinese skipped that stage altogether. In both countries the preference for the single block was as much aesthetic as practical: the reflection of a culture in which the appearance of the writing constituted part of the image, and readers had learned to look at the words as well as through them.

Printed images travel easily, however, even if texts await translation. The impact of Japanese prints on nineteenth-century Europe is an old story, but Dowd’s juxtaposition of a poster that Pierre Bonnard designed to advertise Debray’s champagne in 1891 with a ukiyo-e print of a Kabuki actor that Toyohara Kunichika created twenty-five years earlier provides an eye-catching reminder of just how much Western artists learned from their Eastern counterparts. The large black characters of “France-Champagne” that curve boldly across the top of the poster might almost be said to speak Japanese, as they echo the calligraphic outlines of the curly-headed woman and the champagne bubbles that spill from her glass. At virtually the same time, an elaborate print from 1894 celebrating Japan’s victory in the first land battle of the Sino-Japanese War suggests that Western style was also leaving its mark on the East, as several journalists wearing European dress cluster in one corner, two of them busily recording the action live on their drawing boards. Meanwhile the creator of the print, Mizuno Toshikata, apparently remained in Tokyo, working the whole thing up from published accounts, photographs, and his own imagination.

Advertisement

East Asian cartooning, too, absorbed Western influences, from the variations on the satirical weekly Punch that nineteenth-century British expats launched in Japan and briefly in China to the syndicated cartoons from the US that poured into Japan in the 1920s and 1930s. We’ve grown accustomed to thinking of Japanese manga as a booming import—according to Wikipedia, it has been “massively outselling” American comics since the late 2010s—but Reading Pictures suggests that the influence has gone both ways, as modern versions of an older Japanese tradition of graphic narrative were catalyzed by the translated reprints of American strips that readers began to consume almost a hundred years earlier.

An evocative juxtaposition of a 1931 travel poster inviting tourists to explore the romance and beauty of French Indochina with a Vietnamese propaganda poster produced thirty-five years later suggests how tangled these lines of visual transmission could become, as the Japanese-inflected style of Bonnard and others made its way into the curriculum of the colonial art school in Hanoi, where the designer of the travel poster, Jos-Henri Ponchin, taught Đường Ngọc Cảnh, the Vietnamese artist whose arresting image of a young girl with a lotus and an M16 exhorted her compatriots to “Look after the Land, Look after the Youth.” The young woman in Ponchin’s travel poster holds an umbrella rather than an M16, and she carries it at a slightly more relaxed angle than does her counterpart, but the echoes of color and pattern between the two images are nonetheless striking.

Such cross-cultural comparisons are among the rewards of Reading Pictures, even if they threaten to compound the rather dizzying effect of the whole, with its profusion of images and multiplying narratives. No history, of course, really has a singular origin, but Dowd can’t quite seem to decide which of his many chronologies he wishes to highlight. After an initial survey of early modern printing and publishing, he opens his chapter on the visualization of literature with a familiar episode in the history of the British novel: the serendipitous sequence of events by which Charles Dickens came to write The Pickwick Papers (1836–1837) and stumbled on the formula for illustrated fiction that he and his publishers continued to exploit for the rest of his career.

The story, in more than one sense, began when Dickens was invited to compose the text for a series of sporting prints by the caricaturist Robert Seymour, to be issued monthly on the model of Pierce Egan’s best-selling Life in London (1821), a picaresque narrative that had been printed alongside engravings by George and Robert Cruikshank. Dickens was then a little-known journalist and parliamentary reporter—not yet one to class himself among the “important novelists,” as Dowd seems to think—and the assignment was basically hackwork. Seymour took for granted that his was the principal responsibility in the enterprise, but the new recruit had other ideas, and by the second issue he was requesting significant alterations to one of the artist’s designs. Already at risk of bankruptcy and now facing this additional threat to his autonomy, Seymour redrew the plate in question and promptly shot himself through the heart.

The result was not only that Hablot Knight Browne (better known as “Phiz”) was eventually hired in his place but that Dickens seized control of the project, significantly altering the ratio of text to images and turning a series of episodic sketches into a novel. With the introduction in the fourth issue of the hero’s irresistible sidekick, Sam Weller, the work really took off, and Pickwick became a best seller. The format Dickens had adopted—thirty-two-page monthly numbers with two illustrations each—became standard for Victorian fiction through the middle of the century. Seymour’s “fatal surrender,” as Dowd puts it, also marked a change in the relation between writers and illustrators, with writers now firmly in charge, while illustrators—of literary works at least—were understood as “valuable, fundamentally responsive contributors, decisively bound to an authorial text.”

That understanding of illustration probably remains the dominant one among readers of literature, even if they no longer expect to consume their fiction in monthly issues. It’s also the understanding that governs Dowd’s appealing chapter on children’s books, whose illustrations include a page from a fifteenth-century Chinese primer and a spread from Nu Dang and His Kite (1959)—a sophisticated picture book about a boy in Thailand created by the textile and fashion designer Jacqueline Ayer—as well as some prime examples from what’s been called the golden age of children’s literature: John Tenniel’s frontispiece for Lewis Carroll’s Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland (1865) and a stunning two-page spread of Walter Crane’s chromolithograph for Beauty and the Beast (1875) among them.

Nothing otherwise links Tenniel’s frontispiece to Toshikata’s print of the Japanese army’s victory some three decades later, but it’s nonetheless striking how both men register their self-consciousness about art making by including figures of artists at work within their images. For Tenniel, it’s a frog slyly posed at the right-hand edge of the frame, where he’s apparently serving as the courtroom artist for the King and Queen of Hearts and the bird-headed judges arranged below.

Variations on this conceit seem to have appealed to other illustrators too. Dowd reproduces a cover created by Norman Rockwell for The Saturday Evening Post in 1961, for instance, that pictures the graphic designer Herb Lubalin at work on the magazine’s new logo, as discarded attempts dot the drawing board and old Post covers fan out behind it. Rockwell’s image of the designer at work in turn recalls a cover entitled “Blank Canvas (Deadline)” that he had produced for the same magazine more than two decades earlier, in which the artist pictured himself in the act of inventing—or rather, failing to invent—the cover in question. Yet another mischievous cover, this one by George Lois for a 1963 issue of Esquire, depicts a large billboard of Elizabeth Taylor and Richard Burton in Cleopatra—itself, Dowd notes, an illustration from the film’s poster—with two Lilliputian men perched on a scaffold in front of it. The men are soberly dressed, which adds to the comedy, since they also prove to be working artists, one of whom consults a reference image and draws a further line down Taylor’s cleavage.

Publications like these figure prominently in Dowd’s story. By the turn of the twentieth century the serial format popularized by Dickens had largely died out in Britain and America, and most serious writers of literature seem to have shared James’s desire to keep their pages free of other people’s images. But illustrated fiction for adults remained a significant feature of the general interest magazines that began to invade the market in the 1890s, their success buoyed by the advertisements that increasingly provided their chief source of revenue. Recent advances in photomechanical reproduction also contributed to their popularity, by enabling publishers to swap out engravings for more visually alluring halftones. Employing many of the same artists who also worked anonymously for their advertisers, magazines like McClure’s, Cosmopolitan, and their descendants in the mid-twentieth century encouraged readers to move seamlessly between both kinds of image, especially since “full-page ads,” as Dowd observes, “often included columns of copy and looked like stories.” It may be an accident that Dowd’s own eye seems to have been drawn more to the ads and magazine covers than to the pictures that accompanied the fiction inside, but his preference is also a reminder of how brief, comparatively speaking, was the era when illustrators took their marching orders from the writers of literature. Though Dowd occasionally writes as if illustration were by definition a subordinate activity—most notably, if oddly, when he refers in passing to “the practice of writers illustrating engravings with textual compositions” or adopts the same idiom for the captioning of the cartoons on the back page of The New Yorker—the majority of illustrations in Reading Pictures appear to argue otherwise.

In titling another chapter of his book “Illustrator as Author,” however, Dowd further complicates his narrative, even as he partly revises the chronology he has previously traced by beginning with Dickens. Rather than Phiz’s illustrations for Pickwick, this account opens with William Hogarth and his successful campaign to extend British copyright protection to printed multiples of visual art. The creator of A Harlot’s Progress (1732) had already turned author in Dowd’s sense by telling the tale of a young woman’s seduction and ruin through a sequence of elaborately captioned prints, themselves derived from oil paintings. But engravings like these were vulnerable to counterfeiters, and it was only with the passage of the Engraving Copyright Act of 1734 that Hogarth felt reasonably in control of his market—an achievement that constitutes a seminal moment in the history of printed images and that the artist soon celebrated by issuing another of his famous sequences, The Rake’s Progress (1735).*

Abundantly supplemented by text and filled with emblematic details that require decoding, Hogarth’s prints are clearly pictures to be read. Whether most people would identify them as illustrations is more debatable, but it is this expansive sense of the term that appears to account for many of the other examples in Dowd’s book, from newspaper cartoons and comic strips to manga and graphic novels. Or perhaps it would be more accurate to say that the title Reading Pictures is finally a better guide to Dowd’s project than his subtitle, particularly since he acknowledges at one point that “freestanding” images like cartoons or caricatures don’t really qualify, even as he continues to reproduce a number of these, together with other freestanding images, from posters to the occasional oil painting.

Though Hogarth chiefly figures here as a champion of illustrators’ intellectual property, his visual legacy is abundantly evident as well. Among the most strikingly Hogarth-like of the images in Dowd’s book is a full-page reproduction of a cartoon feature by R.F. Outcault entitled “What they did to the dog-catcher in Hogan’s Alley” that appeared in Joseph Pulitzer’s New York World in 1896 (see illustration at top of article). The cartoon’s action takes place on New York’s Lower East Side rather than in Georgian London, but its raucous urban scene still owes an obvious debt to the eighteenth-century satirist. So, too, does the sheer proliferation of detail—the flames bursting from the dogcatcher’s van, the parrot squawking in a cage suspended from the bars of a fire escape, the boy tumbling headlong into the crowd—as well as the verbal glosses that Outcault scatters, as Hogarth did before him, throughout his image. The advertisement for “McSwat’s New Gold Cure” affixed to the tenement wall is pure Hogarth, as are the lyrics of “The Park Row Songster” that lie on the ground between two dogs and spell out “Its Funny How They Roast Us When We’er Gone [sic],” especially since the dogs’ eager postures and gaping jaws make them look as if they were singing along. We might almost be looking at Hogarth’s Beer Street (1751), Gin Lane (1751), or one of The Four Stages of Cruelty (1751), though the youthful denizens of Hogan’s Alley vigorously beating the dogcatcher to keep him from turning his catch into sausage are likely to evoke far more sympathy than the children torturing dogs and other animals in the first plate of the Four Stages of Cruelty. Outcault is a less sophisticated artist than Hogarth, and his lines lack the other’s refinement, but he clearly belongs in the great printmaker’s lineage.

Dowd also highlights Outcault’s role in the evolution of the comic strip, especially after the cartoonist left Pulitzer’s paper for William Randolph Hearst’s New York Journal, where he began experimenting with telling stories in multiple panels and supplying the parrot—a favorite character, apparently—with speech bubbles. If this practice of narrating primarily through images turns the creators of comic strips and graphic novels into “author-illustrators,” in Dowd’s coinage, then the illustrations they produce are no longer the handmaidens of text but something more like its master.

One of the last examples in Reading Pictures is a page from the graphic novel It’s a Good Life, If You Don’t Weaken (1996) by the Canadian cartoonist known as Seth that virtually does away with words altogether. There’s a speech bubble in the upper left-hand panel, but apart from a street sign spelling out “Milner” at the bottom, the other five panels are wordless: a device the artist employs repeatedly in the course of the narrative, sometimes for several pages at a stretch. The effect is not quite as stark, admittedly, as that produced by one of Dowd’s earliest examples, an initial miniature from a fifteenth-century antiphony in the Siena Cathedral whose vividly painted image of Jesus healing the leper visually overwhelms the capital R of its frame.

But the graphic novel, too, plays with the possibility that “looking,” as Dowd says of the miniature, “is more important than reading,” or at least that looking can itself be a means of reading—as of course it always is. Though Dowd doesn’t explicitly register the fact, the hand lettering of a graphic novel like It’s a Good Life also hearkens back to earlier practices. The comparatively simple strokes with which Seth forms his letters may seem a long way from the fluidity and sophistication of the ideograms in the Diamond Sutra, but both the calligrapher and the cartoonist know that the writer’s mark making can also be part of the picture.

antlers bud blood-pink twelve points

rise with woman pain always the escaped

smell of iron and shame I stain

serve sore at table in apron whites pour wine

fork meat diners finger silver

knives around this heartbeat centerpiece

of one’s own rack thorned and tender

the curious read my roses there

a dozen tines hardened

one for each lunar month each apostle

each egg in a box a bone curl for each step of away

from lush life when sheet ghosts wilt

down to milk of All Souls’ Day

mortal most scarlet

injury jackstraw arrows fly at my

cry-alive and God

entries.title: ‘Reality Has Proved Treacherous’
entries.summary: A new novel recounts Penelope Fitzgerald’s strange sojourn in Mexico in the early 1950s, when her matter-of-fact despair was just coming into view.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
“What was she doing in Mexico?” asks Hermione Lee in her biography of Penelope Fitzgerald.1 In October 1952, decades before Fitzgerald became one of the most celebrated British novelists of the twentieth century, she and her five-year-old son, Valpy, sailed from England to New York City and took a bus south of the border, where they remained until January 1953. Fitzgerald’s husband, Desmond, and their two-year-old daughter, Tina, stayed behind. Fitzgerald was pregnant with their third child, Maria, who was born a couple of months after she and Valpy returned.

In a 1980 essay called “Following the Plot,” Fitzgerald briefly describes her time in Mexico, which she says she wanted to use as the basis for a novel. The voyage, she writes, was proposed by “two old ladies called Delaney” from a Mexican city named Fonseca. The women

lived comfortably, in spite of recent economic reforms, on the proceeds of the family silver mine…. Their relations in Ireland had died, they were alone in the world, and it was hoped that because of some distant friendship they might take kindly to my son and leave him all their money.

The Fitzgeralds’ stay quickly turned into a farce. The old women “were drinking themselves steadily to death.” Residents of Fonseca who were also angling for their wealth “wanted to get rid of me and my son as soon as possible.” Penelope and Valpy were blamed for an accidental death, and they departed “without a legacy, but knowing what it was to be hated.”

When Fitzgerald began publishing novels in the late 1970s, she drew on her odder experiences: working at the BBC during World War II (Human Voices), living on a houseboat in London (Offshore), teaching at a school for child actors (At Freddie’s). The Mexico trip certainly sounds like a promising kernel for one of her dark comedies of ineptitude, self-delusion, and the strange dynamics of small communities. But the story was already too much like fiction. “I could never make it respectable (by which I mean probable) enough to be believed as a novel,” she writes. “Reality has proved treacherous.”

In the biography, Lee is skeptical of Fitzgerald’s account, especially since there’s no place in Mexico called Fonseca: “It sounds, as she says herself, like ‘a yarn,’ a play by Tennessee Williams or a story by Conrad.” Lee seems not to have turned up evidence of the old women or their legacy, but she notes that “the details of the story match the facts about the Saltillo area,” where Valpy remembers going. Saltillo, a city in northeastern Mexico near Monterrey, is “where there were silver mines, and where many Irish and English émigrés settled.”

Then why did Fitzgerald disguise the city? Fonseca is the name of a phantom island that for hundreds of years appeared on European maps of the Caribbean. Could the tale Fitzgerald tells in “Following the Plot” have been a put-on, a phantom story created for an essay about how made-up stories work? Or was the name, which means “dry well” in Latin, a joke about her fruitless efforts both to win the inheritance and to turn the trip into fiction?

Jessica Francis Kane’s daring novel Fonseca is not an attempt to write the book Fitzgerald couldn’t but an effort to figure out why she failed to write it. Drawing on Lee’s biography, the scant details Fitzgerald gave about the journey, and Kane’s own recent correspondence with Valpy and Tina, she imagines the Fitzgeralds’ stay in Mexico with the Delaneys. Fonseca throws Penelope and Valpy into a mysterious, unsettling place where the rules of etiquette are inscrutable, the social masks grotesque, and reality more treacherous than Penelope at first understands.

Some critics have pronounced Fitzgerald’s economical and precise novels—with their keen yet icy emotional insight, careful attention to the physical world, and lightly worn certainty that our lives might at any time tip over into travesty—as close to perfection as the form can get. Any attempt to emulate her style seems certain to fall short. Kane, an American writer who has published two story collections and two previous novels, includes plenty of Fitzgeraldian touches but wisely avoids imitation. Fonseca never really feels like a Fitzgerald book; at times it’s more like a mid-nineteenth-century novel—say, an exoticized cross between Villette and Great Expectations: secrets and simmering hostilities, an inheritance plot, moldering old women in a “shuttered mansion,” and an observant protagonist in a foreign land who’s at once cautious and headstrong.

As a novel about a well-known writer, Fonseca has a clear affinity with The Blue Flower, Fitzgerald’s novel about the German Romantic poet Novalis. An intensely private person, she may have been horrified to see the epigraph from that book, Novalis’s statement that “novels arise out of the shortcomings of history,” applied to herself. But the Mexico trip is an excellent subject for speculation. Kane sets out to answer Lee’s question—What was she doing there?—and to solve the great puzzle of Fitzgerald’s life: With a brilliant undergraduate degree from Oxford, accomplished early work as a critic, and ambitions to write literary fiction, why did she not publish anything between 1953 and 1975 besides the text of an illustrated children’s serial called Jassy of Juniper Farm and an introduction to a posthumous collection of verse by her father, Edmund “Evoe” Knox, a comic poet and the editor of Punch?

Advertisement

The obvious answer is that she had to care and provide for her three children and her husband, who struggled with alcoholism, and that she wasn’t able to return to writing until after her kids had grown up. Fitzgerald herself claimed, not very believably, that she started writing her first novel, the satirical mystery The Golden Child, merely to entertain Desmond during the illness that led to his death in 1976. Kane looks for a deeper explanation. “I think every period makes sacrifices of a certain kind of person,” Fitzgerald said. “I am drawn to people who seem to have been born defeated, or even profoundly lost.” Fonseca proposes that the Mexico journey plunged Fitzgerald into doubt about her ability to achieve lifelong goals and that the winter of 1952 was when she came to see herself as one of the lost and defeated—an “exterminatee,” as she later called her characters.

In the early 1950s she was worrying about money, possibly more than she ever had. Her upbringing in the formidably accomplished but middle-class Knox family likely led her to believe that even if an intellectual career wouldn’t make her rich, it would provide for her needs. Her uncle Dillwyn was a Cambridge papyrologist who during both world wars worked as a military codebreaker. Ronald, another uncle, was a Roman Catholic monsignor, prominent writer, and Oxford chaplain. A third uncle, Wilfred, was an Anglo-Catholic priest who took a vow of poverty and became a chaplain and fellow at Cambridge. “All of them,” Kane writes, “right back to her bishop grandfathers”—Edmund Knox, the bishop of Manchester, and Edward Hicks, the bishop of Lincoln—“distrusted wealth. But bishops and professors were given housing.”

It must have been a shock to Fitzgerald that she encountered financial difficulties despite having a job her family would have approved of. In August 1950 she and Desmond took over World Review, a small British monthly. (Desmond had trained as a lawyer, was a decorated officer in World War II, and in 1949 published a history of his regiment.) During their brief editorship, they turned World Review into an ideal little magazine: wide ranging, cosmopolitan, and alive to the major issues of their time. In addition to covering global affairs, they published essays and dispatches by Albert Camus, Bertrand Russell, and Patrick Leigh Fermor; critical considerations of Bertolt Brecht, Alfred Jarry, and Francis Bacon; and stories by Muriel Spark, J.D. Salinger, Alberto Moravia, and William Saroyan. Stevie Smith, obstreperous and unpredictable, reviewed new novels in the back of the book. But World Review didn’t sell, and by late 1952 it was struggling to stay afloat. So were Fitzgerald and Desmond as they tried to raise their young children on a dwindling income.

It remains unclear whether Fitzgerald and her son were actually summoned to Mexico with the prospect of an inheritance. Throughout Fonseca Kane inserts emails from Valpy and Tina in answer to her questions, and Valpy confirms for her—as he seems not to have for Lee—that he and his mother stayed at a Saltillo mansion owned by three (not two) old women named Purcell (not Delaney). Valpy tells Kane he researched the Purcell estate and found that “there were direct heirs,” taking this to mean that “the inheritance does not appear to have been an issue at all.” The trip, then, may have simply been a way for Fitzgerald to get a break from pressures at work and home. (Kane also suggests that she went to Mexico with the hope of gathering material for fiction, possibly out of professional jealousy of Spark, who had just won a prize for a story based on her experiences in Africa.) Nevertheless, Fonseca sticks closely to the account Fitzgerald gives in “Following the Plot.”

Kane’s Penelope expects the matter of the inheritance to be straightforward, the visit a formality. But things go wrong as soon as she and Valpy arrive in Fonseca (Saltillo in all but name), knock on the Delaneys’ door, and learn that Chela, the sisters’ housekeeper, expected just one guest. Chela bluntly tells Penelope to take a bus back to America, but Penelope convinces her that the young boy can’t be left alone.

Advertisement

There’s something otherworldly about the house, which Kane calls Mirando. The two Delaney women—the widow Doña Anita and her sister-in-law, Doña Elena—only ever leave it for Sunday Mass, and until the church doors close behind them the neighborhood birds fall silent. The northeast corner, where Doña Anita’s husband died, has a constant chill. The gothic aspects of Fonseca strike the right note. Fitzgerald loved ghost stories and believed in the existence of the supernatural. (She always maintained that the “rapper” in The Bookshop—who makes banging noises at unpredictable times—was based on a real poltergeist, and she portrays it as if it were just another nuisance, like a neighbor’s radio played too loudly.)

Most evenings the Delaneys host a cocktail hour, attended by Fonseca’s respectable Mexican residents and members of the city’s English-speaking colony. The doñas know these visitors only want their money, but they enjoy having an audience as they drunkenly squabble over the Victrola and play the same maudlin songs again and again. The guests compete for the legacy by proposing grand philanthropic projects. Señor Molina suggests establishing a fleet of bookmobiles. Señor Garza hopes to turn his small collection of taxidermy into a national bird museum. Mrs. Clancy wants to expand her community outreach in surrounding mountain villages. Mrs. Slater plans to turn Mirando itself into an arts center.

With the exception of the sincere Señor Garza, the schemers are clearly motivated not by goodwill but by greed and a selfish desire “to shape Fonseca into something they liked better.” Penelope thinks of these hangers-on as “Pretenders,” a group in which she includes herself. Even though Valpy is the one being considered for the inheritance, she views it as a potential cash infusion for World Review. She’s so concerned about her finances, Kane writes, that “she dreamed of money every night. In fact…it was not uncommon for her thoughts to take the form of an interview with a bank manager.” Yet with so many buzzards circling the old women, she fears she doesn’t stand a chance. When the other Pretenders challenge her to say what she would put the money into, her answer—a literary magazine—is met with laughter.

Penelope has other things on her mind besides the legacy. Before she left England, Desmond had been drinking heavily, and while in Mexico she learns from a friend that he had to be carried home from a pub two nights in a row. In letters to Penelope, Desmond asks for advice on matters related to World Review and proposes schemes for cutting back: having his first drink ten minutes later every evening, limiting himself to one a night, sticking to Guinness. Predictably, none of these resolutions works.

The people at Mirando have heard about, or guessed at, her marital troubles, and to prevent more rumors from spreading, she tries to hide her pregnancy. She begins a clandestine flirtation with another Pretender—a man calling himself Ernest Delaney and claiming to be related to the doñas—in part to even out the distribution of culpability in her marriage and to turn her anger at Desmond on herself. She keeps busy by writing an article about Mexican muralists, which she assigned herself for World Review, and working on a fictionalized story about Mirando, hoping it will help her better understand the strange situation she finds herself in.

Remarkably, traveling with a young boy may be the easiest part of Penelope’s journey. Valpy is a “delightful child”: precocious, friendly, “kind and observant, quiet.” The transatlantic crossing and the long bus ride from New York to Mexico seem to have passed without any major incidents, and he thrives in Fonseca. The servants at Mirando teach him Spanish and let him help out in the kitchen and garden. He joins a local scout group that’s free of the class and racial divisions found elsewhere in the city. But a couple of months into the visit, Penelope starts to betray his trust—losing a rare silver coin that Valpy found in Mirando’s garden and that he naively believes can solve his family’s money troubles—possibly because the pregnancy makes her feel “foggy, out of it, a little irresponsible.” When he gets angry at her for offending the doñas, his composure begins to crack, and he finally seems like a realistic child.2

Kane’s most ingenious move may be her fictionalization of Edward and Jo Hopper, who happened to be in Saltillo at the same time as the Fitzgeralds. There’s no record that they ever met, but in Fonseca Penelope befriends Jo and marvels at the way Edward, in work and life, “edited out…humanity.” Kane’s depiction of the irascible painter measures up to the uncanny celebrity cameos in Fitzgerald’s work, including Noël Coward in At Freddie’s and Antonio Gramsci in Innocence.

Although Fitzgerald never managed a Mexico novel, she did get a few pieces of writing out of her stay there, and Kane borrows freely from them. Two were essays that appeared in the final issue of World Review in the spring of 1953: the article on muralists and a review of a Tate exhibition of Mexican art and culture that includes her observations of the country. She also wrote a short story, “Our Lives Are Only Lent to Us,” about a devastating fire in a Mexican mining town and the English-speaking expatriates who are oblivious to the suffering of its poor residents. Unpublished during her lifetime, “Our Lives Are Only Lent to Us” is distinct from the fiction Penelope is trying to write in Fonseca, but Kane lifts many names from it for her own characters, as if they were the originals of the ones in Fitzgerald’s story. This is a clever nod to Fitzgerald’s habit in her novel manuscripts of using the real names of people on whom her characters were based.

Throughout Fonseca Kane drops in details from Fitzgerald’s novels, as if they had been planted in her mind in the winter of 1952 and lain dormant for decades. Mrs. Slater, with her quest to turn Mirando into an arts center, is a version of the villainous Mrs. Gamart from The Bookshop. Penelope’s inner conversations with a bank manager are inspired by the daydreamed magistrate who grills Nenna in Offshore. Desmond’s plan to push his drinking back ten minutes every night comes from an alcoholic stage actor in At Freddie’s.

These references are generally “securely bedded down,” as Lee describes Fitzgerald’s own knack for fully assimilating research into her characters’ worlds, but there are a few too many of them. In fictionalizing Fitzgerald, Kane set herself a difficult task, one that can’t be accomplished through an accretion of details from Fitzgerald’s work. After six or seven of these Easter eggs, they start to feel like a shortcut, a way for Kane to show familiarity with Fitzgerald without having to dig deeper into her consciousness.

Amid Kane’s attempt to flesh out Fitzgerald’s tale from “Following the Plot,” she often fails to animate Fonseca’s residents, including Penelope. There are flashes of Fitzgerald’s steely wit, as when Penelope tells Ernest Delaney, “Decision is torment for anyone with imagination.” But for the most part Penelope’s mind is oddly free of ideas, of literature, of history, of an active force sifting and sorting and analyzing information—the things that suffuse Fitzgerald’s novels and give them their vitality. It’s true that Fitzgerald says in “Following the Plot” that she was defeated by the Mexico trip, but in Fonseca the struggle to make sense of it is over before it begins. “Stories and facts in Fonseca were hard to separate,” Penelope thinks. We just don’t get a clear picture of her efforts to uncouple them.

Kane’s previous novel, Rules for Visiting, is a sprightly, occasionally essayistic book about middle-aged friendship, narrated in the first person and rarely with more than two people in a given scene. The leap from that book to Fonseca’s slowly paced, close third-person historical fiction with a large, noisy cast would have been difficult even without a beloved writer at its center. Kane shares with Fitzgerald a sensitivity to unusual objects and customs, the quiet vibrancy of plants and pets, the syncopations in the rhythm of daily life. Yet there’s a lack of control over detail and character in Fonseca that tends to overshadow Kane’s similarities to her subject, especially since control is one of Fitzgerald’s most striking qualities.

A generous reading of Fonseca is that its tentativeness reflects that of its main character. Perhaps rightly, Kane gives us a Fitzgerald before the rough edges have been sanded down. Because of the late start to her career, it’s believable that her younger self would still be some ways off from the hard-bitten outlook that shapes her books: all plans fail, all acts of charity do more harm than good, the only chance at happiness is having the dumb luck to be protected from reality by ingenuousness or amour fou. There’s plenty of hypocrisy and preening in Fonseca, but Fitzgerald’s matter-of-fact despair, which so distinguishes her novels from the British comedy of manners, is just starting to come into view.

What Fonseca gets exactly right is that, as in Fitzgerald’s books, its keynote is failure. Penelope proves inept at winning the sympathies of the Delaneys and at resolving the questions Kane raises—about the eerie mansion and its inhabitants, about the identity of Ernest Delaney, about a potentially disastrous development at the doñas’ silver mine. Penelope never does manage to unravel the yarn.

In reality, after Fitzgerald’s return to England, the failures mounted. World Review collapsed, Desmond was disbarred after stealing £373 (about £7,000 today) from his law firm in 1962, and in 1963 her family’s houseboat sank in the Thames. “Do you regret going?” asks Penelope’s inner bank manager at the end of Fonseca, implying that the Mexico trip was what set these later troubles in motion. Penelope replies, “To Fonseca? No. Anyway, Fonseca wasn’t a place…. If anything it was an idea, or a time. It was a dry well. It was certainly the end of a dream and the beginning of a long wait.”

entries.title: Evolution of a Cynic
entries.summary: JD Vance’s new memoir attempts to sidestep the vice-president’s ambitions with a shallow recounting of his conversion to Catholicism.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
JD Vance, the fiftieth vice-president of the United States and a likely Republican nominee for the 2028 presidential election, is the product of an extraordinary degree of self-creation and mythmaking, even by the standards of American political careers. He was born James Donald Bowman, the son of a single mother and a father who left when he was a toddler; at age six, having been adopted by his mother’s new husband, he became James David Hamel; graduating from law school in his late twenties, he took the last name of his beloved grandmother and became J.D. Vance. Even after he found fame with that name—as the author of the multimillion-selling memoir Hillbilly Elegy (2016) and as one of the liberal media’s more prolific anti-Trump pundits—the tinkering continued, though at a more modest scale: when he ran for the Senate in 2021 he did so with a revised first name to go with his new hard-line MAGA political convictions, having dropped the periods between his initials to become JD Vance. This remains, at the time of this writing, the vice-president’s name.

It is not unusual, of course, for an American political career to be built on the foundation of a life story. In 1995, when he was still a young lecturer at the University of Chicago, Barack Obama published his memoir Dreams from My Father, and he became an Illinois state senator the following year. And from the 1980s until the 2010s, first with his book The Art of the Deal and then via the fifteen-season run of NBC’s The Apprentice, Donald Trump cultivated the straight-shooting business savant persona that propelled him to the White House. Perhaps because he lacks the formidable personal presence of either of these predecessors, Vance has built his career to a remarkable degree on narrative foundations.

Hillbilly Elegy was published in June 2016, and its fortunes benefited greatly from the media’s scramble to account for the MAGA movement’s popularity among white working-class voters. Vance, an opportunist of rare instinct and exceptional ruthlessness, retailed hard truths about American society translated into a language the liberal elite wanted to hear. His book took a complicated history of Appalachian poverty and deindustrialization and made of it an American Dream–friendly story of personal redemption and self-determination. By his account, the reasons Appalachian communities were thwarted by social deprivation and addiction had less to do with structural forces—generations of class inequality, dispossession of labor by capital—and more to do with the failure of individuals to extricate themselves from bad situations, as he himself had done with such dramatic success. Vance made his name, in a sense, by speaking for his people with one side of his mouth while condemning them out of the other. “There is a lack of agency here,” he wrote in Hillbilly Elegy, “a feeling that you have little control over your life and a willingness to blame everyone but yourself.”

Writing some kind of memoir is, of course, a nonnegotiable component in the machinery of a high-level American political career. When it comes to presidential races, the number of candidates will invariably be equaled by the number of memoirs, more often than not ghostwritten.* And the reasons for this are not hard to discern: the cultural soil of the United States is famously rich in entrepreneurialism and individualism. If a person is to make something of himself in American life, he must have a sales pitch; he must be able to sing, for the general public, the song of himself and his origins.

And yet Vance is, in certain crucial respects, an outlier: he was a hugely successful writer well before he embarked on any kind of political career. Hillbilly Elegy has a great many literary flaws, but it is by no means a standard campaign meet and greet. We might be tempted to compare it to, say, Obama’s Dreams from My Father, but in fact that book didn’t exactly fly off the shelves when it was first published; Hillbilly Elegy sold hundreds of thousands of copies in its first year and in 2020 was made into a film by Ron Howard starring Amy Adams and Glenn Close. Vance’s publishing-to-politics trajectory seems to me, in this sense, an entirely unique proposition—as though Frank McCourt had parlayed the success of Angela’s Ashes into a Senate run, or as though Eat, Pray, Love had propelled Elizabeth Gilbert all the way to the vice-presidency.

A first-time writer of more ordinary ambition would have followed the success of Hillbilly Elegy with another memoir picking up the thread where that breakout success left off, as McCourt did with ’Tis and Gilbert did with Committed. But there is a limit to the power and prestige that accrue to even the most successful of memoirists. Annie Ernaux won the Nobel Prize for her artful excavations of family and class, but she has never been in a position—nor has she, it should be noted, shown any sign of wanting to be in a position—to negotiate peace deals with Iran or to berate EU leaders for their lax military spending.

Advertisement

And yet as we have said, ambitious politicians do tend to become memoirists; so it is that Vance has returned, via this elaborately indirect route, to his old job, or some version of it. According to a report in Variety in 2017 Tina Bennett, Vance’s then literary agent, negotiated an $8 million publishing deal for a follow-up to Hillbilly Elegy. Communion both is and, in many notable ways, is not that follow-up. Vance has said that he began writing it in 2017, well before he entered politics. The reason the book took so long to complete is self-evident, and certainly more impressive than most writers’ excuses for not turning in a manuscript on time. The reason that it’s finally being published now, in 2026, is just as clear: its author very much wishes to become the next president of the United States.

Communion presents itself as an account of Vance’s personal journey to the Catholic faith. In this sense, it really is a follow-up to Hillbilly Elegy, which was the story of his personal journey from the Appalachian working class to the elite realms of Yale Law School and venture capital. Like that book, Communion is characterized by its author’s almost obsessive self-positioning as an outsider, as a man who gained entry to the cloisters of those coastal elites and who has nothing but contempt for the careerism and hypocrisy he encountered there.

Vance makes frequent displays of self-criticism, often depicting himself in his younger days as unthinkingly prostrate before the false liberal-elite god of professional advancement. “At some point in my university career, my desire for stability morphed into a craving for conquest,” he writes. “I didn’t just want a nice car, a house, and a decent vacation. I wanted to win for winning’s sake.” This early part of the book is filled with the sort of stranger-in-a-strange-land shtick that will be familiar to readers of his earlier memoir. (One of the chapters is, in fact, entitled “Stranger in a Strange Land.”) He parses the complicated prestige economy he observed at Yale, where, because everyone is already assumed to be wealthy, social status is derived not from owning a large vacation home or from securing a position at a prestigious private equity firm but instead from getting a White House job or a federal appeals court clerkship. “But prestige, interestingly enough, never flowed from the nonprofessional parts of life,” as he puts it in one of the book’s many grotesquely faux-naive passages.

No one discussed family life with the same level of pride with which they announced their fancy jobs. In other words, prestige could be accumulated through professional choices and accomplishments. But being a good mother or a good husband wasn’t valued nearly as highly as achieving a new credential, being admitted to a top school, or getting a great job.

This sort of thing is risible enough, of course, but it is downright absurd when you reflect, as any sentient reader must, on the writer, who is one of the most nakedly careerist public figures in living memory. And this is where Communion—which I will say now, in order to get it out of the way, is a very bad and boring book, in ways that greatly exceed even the badness and boringness of Hillbilly Elegy—gets interesting, if not to read then certainly to think about. Precisely because it is so bad and boring, I found myself reading it through its author’s palpable desire to become president, and therefore as a book whose true subject can never be acknowledged or even alluded to.

That critique of shallow credentialism and careerism at Yale, for instance, is rendered at once explicable and absurd by the reader’s knowledge of a fact rigorously withheld from the text itself: that Vance is criticizing careerism precisely in service of his own monstrous professional ambition. Once you begin to see this technique as something like an organizing principle, the whole book becomes an exercise in avoidance, like a sort of Oulipo-style experiment in formal constraint.

Vance does allude to what he calls his “evolution from Trump critic to Trump supporter,” but has nothing at all to say on the substance of his own criticisms. It’s left up to a moderately well-informed reader to recall that Vance, whose mother struggled with opioid addiction, referred to Trump in a 2016 Atlantic article as “cultural heroin” and that, in a leaked message to a former Yale roommate, he reportedly said, “I go back and forth between thinking Trump is a cynical asshole like Nixon who wouldn’t be that bad (and might even prove useful) or that he’s America’s Hitler.”

He also says next to nothing about why he pivoted so hard from his original stance. He merely states that the many great successes of Trump’s first term made his former position unsustainable, though he never suggests what these successes might have been. “To my critics,” he writes, “it was a politically cynical maneuver to gain political power. I doubt I’ll ever change their minds.” In fact, he doesn’t try. He contents himself with a kind of autobiographical tautology: his “political evolution,” he claims, “was downstream of the much more fundamental change in how I saw the world. I had looked inside our elite institutions and found them intellectually and spiritually broken. Was it any surprise that I would eventually reject their politics as well?”

To dwell on Vance’s hypocrisy and cynicism here is to risk seeming naive, but the depth of his contempt for the reader is genuinely impressive. Can this man really be claiming that his experience of an intellectually and spiritually broken elite led him to embrace the presidency of Donald Trump? Does he really expect his readers to overlook the lurid venality and corruption of an administration of which he himself is a central figure—to simply forget about the crypto pump-and-dump schemes, the lavish gifts from foreign interests, the vast fortunes amassed by the president and his family in his second term—and unquestioningly accept this abject excuse for a moral rationale? Apparently he does. And he may have good reason for doing so, given that reviewers of his first book, and the liberal media pundit class more generally, swallowed Hillbilly Elegy whole. As Gabriel Winant wrote in a 2023 essay for n+1, the book’s success was symptomatic. It

bespeaks the intellectual and political barrenness of elite liberalism that so many people and institutions—the agent and publisher who got him in print, the Yale faculty who advanced his career, the journalists at outlets like Vox and the New York Times who reviewed him favorably, the politicians like Hillary Clinton who praised his work—failed to see what he was doing straightaway.

Not only does Vance fail to provide any kind of serious account of his political conversion, but he devotes strikingly little energy to Trump at all. In one sense, it could be argued that this omission makes sense and is even necessary, given that Communion is framed as a reflection on religion and specifically Vance’s conversion to Catholicism. But the book is at most partly that, and even in the passages in which he attempts to engage in some depth with the questions of religious faith, the writing is almost entirely defined by what’s not said. Vance makes basically no attempt, for instance, to reconcile the Trump administration’s extraordinary and deliberate cruelty toward immigrants (not to mention its starting a war with Iran, or its support of a genocide in Gaza) with the explicit teachings of Christ.

It’s worth recalling that, mere days after becoming vice-president, Vance got embroiled in a public conflict with the Vatican on exactly this subject. In January 2025, in an interview on Fox News, he invoked a garbled version of the Augustinian notion of ordo amoris, the “order of love,” to claim that Christians ought first to love family, then neighbors, then fellow citizens, and only then the rest of the world. Pope Francis responded with a letter to American bishops in which he pointedly clarified that love, for Christians, is not a “concentric expansion of interests that little by little extend to other persons and groups”; rather, he wrote, “the true ordo amoris that must be promoted is that which we discover by meditating constantly on the parable of the ‘Good Samaritan’… that is, by meditating on the love that builds a fraternity open to all, without exception.” Francis’s successor, Pope Leo XIV, has been no less critical of the cruelty and violence of the Trump administration’s foreign policy, pointing out that Jesus “is never on the side of those who once wielded the sword and today drop bombs.” Infamously, Vance responded to that statement by saying that the pope should “be careful” when speaking on matters of theology.

There is something irreducibly comic about Vance making a great public display of his conversion to Catholicism only to immediately, on assuming the office of vice-president, start a high-profile dispute with the actual pope. There is a word for people who dispute the pope’s authority on doctrinal matters, and that word is “Protestant.” And despite his book’s ostensible focus on how and why he became a Catholic, there is really no sense, in these pages, of Vance having any serious spiritual commitment; there is no real engagement with the question of why he chose to join the one, holy, Catholic, and apostolic Church, as opposed to, say, renewing a connection with the evangelical faith of his family (or, for that matter, converting to the Hindu faith in which his Indian American wife, Usha, was raised). He says nothing about the veneration of Mary—aside from noting that it was admired by Charlie Kirk—and his discussion of the sacrament of confession is laughably perfunctory. “The idea of speaking of my sins to a stranger mortified me,” he writes. “Yet our Catholic friend Sam described confession in a way that resonated with me: It’s like therapy, but with less whining and more guilt.”

Similarly, despite the book’s grand title, the sacrament of Communion is afforded just a few brisk sentences. “The word itself comes from the Latin root communio, which means sharing something in common or union or fellowship,” he writes, in the immemorial style of an undergraduate padding out a term paper the night before it’s due. “For Catholics, Communion means not only to personally encounter Christ but to unite us as a single worshiping body.” But even this aspect of the faith—the Mass, coming together, the literal communion—seems to have gained no real purchase on Vance, who writes in the book’s very first lines that “about half the time these days, we attend Mass at home, in the three-story historic mansion where we are living during my term as vice president.” The book has no sooner begun, in other words, than the reader is forced to doubt the seriousness of its author’s commitment to his supposed new faith. In fact, you don’t even have to open the book for these doubts to take hold: as multiple observers have noted, the pretty, white-steepled church featured on its cover is in fact a Methodist house of worship in rural Virginia.

The point here is not that the church happens to belong to a different denomination but that its not being a Catholic church should have been blatantly obvious to anyone who knew the first thing about Catholicism, separated as it is by a famously vast aesthetic chasm from the Low Church Protestant faiths. (Is Vance, as vice-president of the United States, busier than most writers with a book about to come out? Almost certainly. Is he too busy to glance at a cover sent by his publisher for his approval? Certainly not.) If Communion were, in fact, an Oulipo-style exercise in formal constraint—an account of a conversion to Catholicism by a man who isn’t actually a Catholic; a book written in service of a presidential run by a man who cannot give voice to his desire to be president—HarperCollins could have done a lot worse than put such a legibly Methodist church on its cover.

One of the memoir’s more notable negative spaces is that around Peter Thiel, an account of whose influence is vital to any real understanding of Vance’s remarkable career. Thiel is mentioned in the book, but merely in passing; Vance writes of attending a talk he gave at Yale on the connection between shallow and hypercompetitive elites and technological stagnation. Thiel, he writes, “gave voice to something I had been feeling, but had not fully understood: that I was obsessed with achievement per se—not to accomplish something meaningful, but to win a social competition. I had prioritized striving over character, and for what was I even striving?”

The overbearing irony here is that it was Thiel who more than anyone else fueled and facilitated Vance’s striving. Under his influence, Vance decided to forgo a career in law to work in venture capital. In 2016 he became a principal in Thiel’s firm Mithril Capital. In 2019, with Thiel’s backing—along with that of Marc Andreessen, Eric Schmidt, and others—he started his own Ohio-based tech VC firm, Narya. In 2021 Thiel, an early Silicon Valley adopter of the MAGA movement—and a decisive figure in Vance’s “evolution” from Never Trumper to MAGA true believer—brokered a rapprochement between Vance and Trump at Mar-a-Lago. This prepared the ground for Vance’s Senate run the following year, with Trump’s endorsement and with Thiel’s financial backing (at $15 million, the largest such donation in Senate history). According to a report in The Washington Post, when Trump was deliberating on a running mate for the 2024 election, he received multiple calls from Thiel, among other powerful Silicon Valley figures, imploring him to add Vance to the ticket. The Biden presidency was broadly unpopular with Silicon Valley’s investor class, because of its strict regulation of cryptocurrencies and its attempts to regulate the development of artificial intelligence. The calculation—that a Trump presidency with a tech VC on the ticket would rectify the situation—proved correct.

For decades Thiel has been working to reshape the American political system, and as a consequence the international order, according to his postdemocratic ideological convictions. Thiel has infamously claimed that freedom (by which he seems to mean capitalism) is no longer compatible with democracy, and he has advocated for remaking the state in the image of the corporation. His antidemocratic tendencies have, in recent years, been informed by an increasingly extreme conservative Christianity. Last year he gave a series of lectures in which he claimed that environmental regulations and guardrails on developing technology—AI in particular—could prepare the ground for the coming of the Antichrist. (Among his suggestions as to the identity of this Antichrist was Greta Thunberg.)

Thiel’s influence is clearly legible in Vance’s increasingly extreme and illiberal political positions, his opposition to the regulation of AI, his contempt for international institutions, and his venomous antipathy toward universities and academics. “The professors are the enemy,” he said in a 2021 speech, quoting Richard Nixon. “We have to honestly and aggressively attack the universities in this country.” In a podcast interview that same year, he called for a “de-Ba’athification program” for government employees: “We should just seize the administrative state for our own purposes. We should fire…every single mid-level bureaucrat, every civil servant in the administrative state, [and] replace them with our people.” Anyone who is familiar with Thiel’s political positions, or with those of his friend Curtis Yarvin—a far-right blogger who for many years has been among the most influential figures in Silicon Valley’s rightward turn—will recognize the provenance of these ideas and the purpose they serve for Vance as he becomes their vector.

If Communion has a central premise, it’s the fiction of Vance’s apostasy from a hollow secular-liberal faith of prestige and careerism. This vein of pure Thielism is one of the few aspects of the book through which Vance’s real motivation—his own annihilating personal ambition and Thiel’s ideological interests—is laid bare. And that strange emptiness, that lack of character in multiple senses of the word, accounts for much of what is uniquely unsettling about Vance. This is a man who will become a mouthpiece for any political position, who will attach himself to any powerful person he feels will further his own ambitions; this is a man who will betray whomever and whatever it is necessary to betray in order to obtain power.

In one of the countless passages in which Vance claims to see the error of his former ambitious and careerist ways, he borrows a phrase from the opinion columnist David Brooks: résumé virtues. This, he writes, describes “the things that make us more marketable or successful in the professional world (in contrast to the eulogy virtues that people discuss after our deaths).” He was, he tells us, “obsessed with these résumé virtues and running a race I didn’t fully understand. I didn’t care; I just wanted to win.” The passage is a sort of purloined letter, a confession hiding in plain sight, placed there by an author whose work, whose entire political career, is characterized by a blithe contempt for the intelligence of his audience. Vance’s professed Catholicism, a faith he wants us to believe has deposed that former ambition and careerism, is itself nothing more than a résumé virtue, a calculated move in a larger bid for the job he desperately wants and cannot yet admit he wants.

Christ himself had much to say about those who used the outward performance of faith to further their worldly ambition; he wished woe on the “scribes and Pharisees” who strove for the outward appearance of righteousness while being inwardly “full of hypocrisy and iniquity.” To read Communion is to feel strongly that Vance understands himself to be just such a scribe and a Pharisee, just such a whited sepulchre containing nothing but bones and rotted flesh. The Bible passage he repeats more than any other in Communion, blurting it out like a repressed truth that cannot be assimilated by even the most efficient machinery of lies, is Jesus’ teaching recorded in Matthew 7:16–20:

Ye shall know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles? Even so every good tree bringeth forth good fruit; but a corrupt tree bringeth forth evil fruit. A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit, neither can a corrupt tree bring forth good fruit. Every tree that bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire. Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them.

Vance’s book, rotten fruit that it is of his own corruption and of the wider corruption of the system that produced and sustains him, cannot withstand the poetry of these words. Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them. The words on the page burn with a furious dramatic irony, consuming the cheap vanity of this hollow and iniquitous book, reducing it to ash in the reader’s hands.
